newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds, dollar rise on jobs report.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds, dollar rise on jobs report.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds ended sharply higher Friday as the August employment report calmed fears about a sharp rise in interest rates by the Federal Reserve.
However, a belief that rates will still increase slightly boosted the dollar.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 52.90 points at 5,659.86, bouncing back from Thursday's 50-point fall. For the week, the Dow was up 43.65 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,645 to 693 on moderate volume of 348 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Stocks shadowed the rebound in bonds after a key report on hourly wages soothed the frayed nerves of inflation-wary investors.
The 30-year Treasury bond rose more than half a point, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, fell to 7.11 percent from 7.15 percent at Thursday's close.
The market is now betting on a modest rise of one-quarter percentage point in interest rates compared with recent talk that it could be a sharp increase of one-half percentage point.

"We dodged a major bullet," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "At worst we'll see a 25 basis point (one-quarter percentage point) increase at the Sept. 24 meeting."
The Labour Department report said the jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent in August, and non-farm payrolls rose by 250,000, about even with economists' estimates.

The drop in the unemployment rate, brought the jobless rate to its lowest level since March 1989, when it was 5 percent, the department said. Average hourly earnings of workers rose to $11.87 in August from $11.81 in July.

The upward pressure on wages, including a 50-cent-an-hour increase in the government-mandated minimum wage on Oct. 1, comes at a time when prices for food and energy are also showing signs of rising, which could prod the Fed to raise interest rates to stem inflationary pressures.
A decision on raising interest rates could come out of the the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Sept. 24.
Analysts said because stocks and bonds had sold off steeply Thursday out of fear an extremely strong report, traders took solace in the report's merely mildly surprising strength.
"Yesterday, everybody sold off ahead of the numbers and now the numbers came in fairly decent," said Hildegard Zagorski, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
Late Friday, the dollar rose to 109.28 Japanese yen and 1.4920 German marks from 109.20 yen and 1.4863 marks late Thursday.
Heating oil prices led petroleum markets higher Friday on worries about low stocks heading into the winter.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, October heating oil rose 1.37 cents a gallon to close at 66.40 cents. October crude oil settled 41 cents higher at $23.85 a barrel. October gasoline ended up 0.86 cent at 65.27 cents a gallon.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices jumped higher for a second straight day amid worries about dry weather. November soybeans closed up 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $8, a six-week high.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index finished up 5.8 points at 3,893.0, up 25.3 from last week. In Tokyo, the key 225-share Nikkei average closed down 227.29 points or 1.12 percent at 20,152.53, a drop of 14.37 on the week.
